newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong airfreight market faces competition.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong airfreight market faces competition.

text.p: - Increased competition for Hong Kong's air cargo business could eventually come from rival airports on both sides of the Pearl River estuary, especially if these offer cheaper fees and the same level of efficiency as Hong Kong, Indoswiss Aviation managing director, Jim Eckes said on Monday.

Most of China's air cargo business is generated from its coastal provinces. Investment in airports close to Hong Kong will offer shippers -- manufacturers and exporters-- advantages, "but their efficiency for routing air cargo must approach that of Kai Tak.... and this could take 10 years," he told the Asian Air Cargo conference.

"Why should goods be trucked to Hong Kong for shipment by air with all the paperwork costs and time involved at border crossings when it would be much simpler to fly them directly from southern China," he added.

But Hong Freight Forwarders Association vice chairman, Anthony Lau said Hong Kong air cargo is expected to continue to grow after 1997 as the most likely scenario is for the succesful implemenation of "one country, two systems" and that Hong Kong "will remain as the gateway to China for many years to come."

Hong Kong's airfreight throughout is forecast to grow at an annual average of 8.1 percent a year between 1997 and 2015. By then, what is today the world's second largest international air cargo centre, will be handling 16,069 tonnes daily, "enough to fill 80 jumbos freighters with a full load in and out of Chek Lap Kok every day," he added.
Already airfreight from China represents more than 69 percent of Hong Kong's total export tonnage, Lau said.
"The other Pearl River airports will draw in traffic once they are able to handle cargo efficiently," Eckes said.

These are Macau which opened in November 1995, China's most modern airport at Zhuhai (close to Macau and a potential rival), Shenzhen (close to Hong Kong) and Guangzhou's new US$4 billion airport due to open in 2001, Eckes added.

Already Macau is having some impact on Hong Kong as it is handling carriers unable to get any or sufficient traffic rights at Kai Tak and this will grow when it has dedicated cargo facility, Eckes said.

Macau can for the time being draw in traffic from Zhuhai and the surrounding Greater Zhuhai region, but the local government is likely to press to make Zhuhai an international aiport as foreign investment moves in, he said.
"This will mean added pressure on Macau to generate business."

Shenzhen airport, close to Hong Kong, is the country's second most modern airport and already China's fifth busiest although only opened four years ago. It is building up its air cargo business from the east of the Pearl River estuary, he said.
The new Guangzhou airport will have two runways, with expansion plan for two more and "hopefully the designers will build a cargo facility to match that at Kai Tak," Eckes said.

HAFFA's Lau said that a stable environment after 1997 "will motivate the business community in Hong Kong to continue to invest in Guangdong Province (adjoining Hong Kong) which will demand airfreight space."

"With improved facilities, service standards and lower operating costs, Guangzhou airport will attract a lot of airfreight which would otherwise be shipped through Hong Kong," Lau added. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
